title: How do you implement tiered retries for transient failures using retry topics (main → `retry.1s` → `retry.5s` → `retry.30s` → DLQ, graduating a message to the next topic each time it fails) instead of blocking the main consumer, and why use exponential backoff + jitter (to avoid a thundering-herd retry storm) while classifying transient (retry) vs permanent (straight to DLQ) failures?
shortTitle: Tiered retries with retry topics, exponential backoff with jitter, and transient vs permanent classification

s1_definition.profdef: Tiered retries with retry topics are a non-blocking retry pattern where a failed record is not retried in place on the main consumer but is republished to a dedicated retry topic whose consumer is delayed. If it fails again, it graduates to the next retry topic with a longer delay, and after the last tier it goes to a dead letter queue. Each retry topic adds a fixed delay, so the overall schedule approximates exponential backoff, and adding jitter spreads retries in time to avoid a thundering-herd storm where many records retry at the same instant. Failures are classified first: transient failures enter the retry pipeline, while permanent failures skip it and go straight to the dead letter queue.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's settlement desk hitting a temporary outage in the credit bureau. Instead of the clerk freezing on one form while the bureau is down, the form is dropped into a "try again in 1 second" tray, then a "try again in 5 seconds" tray, then a "try again in 30 seconds" tray, each handled by a different clerk who only picks up forms after the delay. If it still fails, it goes to the problem tray. Jitter is like telling clerks not to all retry at the exact same tick, so they do not stampede the bureau the moment it recovers. And a form with a clearly invalid account number skips all the trays and goes straight to the problem tray, because retrying will never help.
s1_definition.oneliner: Graduate transient failures through delayed retry topics with exponential backoff plus jitter so the main consumer never blocks, and send permanent failures straight to the dead letter queue.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Tiered retries with retry topics are a non-blocking retry pattern where a failed record is not retried in place on the main consumer but is republished to a dedicated retry topic whose consumer is delayed. If it fails again, it graduates to the next retry topic with a longer delay, and after the last tier it goes to a dead letter queue. Each retry topic adds a fixed delay, so the overall schedule approximates exponential backoff, and adding jitter spreads retries in time to avoid a thundering-herd storm where many records retry at the same instant. Failures are classified first: transient failures enter the retry pipeline, while permanent failures skip it and go straight to the dead letter queue.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India's settlement desk hitting a temporary outage in the credit bureau. Instead of the clerk freezing on one form while the bureau is down, the form is dropped into a "try again in 1 second" tray, then a "try again in 5 seconds" tray, then a "try again in 30 seconds" tray, each handled by a different clerk who only picks up forms after the delay. If it still fails, it goes to the problem tray. Jitter is like telling clerks not to all retry at the exact same tick, so they do not stampede the bureau the moment it recovers. And a form with a clearly invalid account number skips all the trays and goes straight to the problem tray, because retrying will never help.

**One line to remember:** Graduate transient failures through delayed retry topics with exponential backoff plus jitter so the main consumer never blocks, and send permanent failures straight to the dead letter queue.

sections.s2_technical:
The problem with retrying in place is that a blocking retry on the main consumer stalls the whole partition while it sleeps between attempts, so one slow record delays everything behind it. Tiered retry topics solve this by moving the waiting off the main consumer. When a record fails, the main consumer immediately publishes it to a retry topic and commits, so the main partition keeps moving. A separate consumer on the retry topic applies the delay for that tier before attempting again.

The tiers form a graduating ladder. A common layout is the main topic, then retry.1s, retry.5s, retry.30s, then the dead letter queue. Each tier has a longer delay, so the total wait grows roughly geometrically, which is exponential backoff: wait a little, then more, then a lot. This gives a transient dependency time to recover without hammering it immediately. The record carries a header counting how many attempts it has had, and each failure increments it and moves the record to the next tier; when it exhausts the last tier, it goes to the dead letter queue.

Exponential backoff alone has a flaw: if many records failed at the same moment because a dependency went down, they will all retry at the same moment when their identical delays elapse, creating a thundering herd that knocks the dependency over again just as it recovers. Jitter fixes this by adding a random spread to each delay, for example a one-second tier actually waiting somewhere between 0.5 and 1.5 seconds, so retries are smeared across time and the recovering dependency sees a gentle ramp instead of a spike.

Classification is the gate in front of the whole pipeline. Transient failures, like a database timeout, a temporary network error, or a dependency returning a retryable status, belong in the retry ladder because waiting may help. Permanent failures, like a validation error, a deserialization failure, or a business rule rejection, will never succeed no matter how many times you retry, so you send them straight to the dead letter queue and do not waste tiers on them.

In Spring Kafka this pattern is built in with the `@RetryableTopic` annotation, where you set attempts, a backoff with a multiplier, and exceptions to treat as not retryable, and Spring auto-creates the retry topics and the dead letter topic. The senior nuances are that non-blocking retry topics preserve main-partition throughput, that ordering is relaxed because a retried record is delivered later than its neighbors, so this pattern suits records that do not require strict ordering, and that every tier and the dead letter topic must be monitored. Jitter should always accompany exponential backoff in a system with correlated failures, which banks have because dependencies fail for whole populations of records at once.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's settlement consumer calls a credit bureau that occasionally times out for a few seconds. Retrying in place would freeze the partition during every backoff. This is exactly the case for non-blocking tiered retry topics: move the waiting off the main consumer.

Problem 2 — When the bureau went down, thousands of records failed at once, and a naive fixed backoff made them all retry together and re-crash the bureau the instant it came back. This is exactly why exponential backoff with jitter is needed: spread the retries so the recovering dependency is not stampeded.

Problem 3 — Some records fail because the account id is structurally invalid, which will never succeed. This is exactly the permanent-failure case: skip the retry ladder and go straight to the dead letter queue.

We simulate the ladder in plain Java. A `RetryRouter` classifies a failure, computes the delay for the tier with exponential backoff and jitter, and moves the record to the next retry topic or the dead letter queue. The demo runs a transient failure through 1s, 5s, 30s tiers to the dead letter queue, and a permanent failure straight to the dead letter queue. The code will show: a `Message`, a `FailureType`, a `BackoffCalculator` with jitter, a `RetryRouter`, and a demo.

```yaml
# application.yml — Spring @RetryableTopic auto-creates retry + dlt topics
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: localhost:9092
    consumer:
      group-id: settlement
      enable-auto-commit: false
# Example listener config (Java):
#   @RetryableTopic(attempts = "4",
#       backoff = @Backoff(delay = 1000, multiplier = 5.0),  // 1s,5s,25s...
#       dltStrategy = DltStrategy.FAIL_ON_ERROR,
#       exclude = { ValidationException.class })             // permanent -> straight to DLT
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transient failure for trade TRD-001 and a permanent failure for TRD-777.

Step 1: TRD-001 fails on the main topic with a transient credit-bureau timeout. The router classifies it transient, computes a delay of roughly one second with jitter, and routes it to retry.1s, incrementing its attempt count to one. The main consumer has already committed and moved on, so the partition never blocked.

Step 2: TRD-001 fails again on retry.1s. The router computes roughly five seconds with jitter and routes it to retry.5s, attempts now two.

Step 3: TRD-001 fails again on retry.5s. The router computes roughly twenty-five seconds with jitter and routes it to retry.30s, attempts now three.

Step 4: TRD-001 fails on retry.30s. The router sees the attempt count has exhausted the ladder, so it routes the record to the dead letter topic transfers.DLT for inspection.

Step 5: TRD-777 fails on the main topic with an invalid account id, which the router classifies permanent. It skips the entire retry ladder and goes straight to transfers.DLT, because retrying a structurally invalid record would only waste the tiers.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Tiered retries with retry topics are how I retry transient failures without ever blocking the main consumer. The problem with retrying in place is that sleeping between attempts on the main partition stalls every record behind the failing one. Instead, when a record fails transiently, the main consumer immediately republishes it to a dedicated retry topic and commits, so the main partition keeps flowing, and a separate consumer on the retry topic applies that tier's delay before trying again. The record graduates through a ladder, for example main, then retry.1s, then retry.5s, then retry.30s, and if it still fails after the last tier it lands in the dead letter queue.

The reason the delays grow is exponential backoff: a transient dependency usually needs a little time to recover, so waiting a short time, then longer, then longer still, gives it room without hammering it. But exponential backoff alone has a failure mode. When a dependency goes down, a whole population of records fails at the same instant, and with identical delays they all retry at the same instant when the delay elapses, which is a thundering herd that re-crashes the dependency the moment it recovers. Jitter fixes this by adding a random spread to each delay, so a one-second tier might actually wait anywhere from half a second to a second and a half, smearing the retries across time so the recovering dependency sees a gentle ramp.

In front of the whole pipeline I classify the failure. Transient failures like a timeout or a temporary network error go into the retry ladder because waiting may help. Permanent failures like a validation error or a deserialization failure will never succeed, so they skip the ladder and go straight to the dead letter queue, which keeps me from wasting tiers on a record that is simply wrong. In Spring Kafka I get this almost for free with the RetryableTopic annotation, setting the attempts, a backoff with a multiplier, and the exceptions to exclude as non-retryable, and Spring auto-creates the retry and dead letter topics.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, our settlement consumer calls a credit bureau that sometimes times out, and when it went fully down thousands of records failed together. With tiered retry topics, exponential backoff, and jitter, the main partition never blocks during retries, the failed records spread their retries across the recovery window instead of stampeding the bureau, and records that are permanently invalid go straight to the dead letter topic. The one caveat I always state is that this pattern relaxes ordering, because a retried record arrives later than its neighbors, so I apply it to records that do not require strict ordering, and I monitor every tier and the dead letter topic. The senior framing is that this turns a flaky dependency from a partition-wide outage into a background, self-pacing recovery that protects both my throughput and the dependency itself.
